My dear sirs and madams,    It is with great admiration and considerable awe that I commit to paper my most favourable impressions of a remarkable technological marvel—a pastime so enthralling, so spirited, so resplendent with daring and strategy, that it has quite captured the very essence of modern digital amusement. I speak, of course, of the venerable and thrilling enterprise known as Counter-Strike 2, the successor to the already beloved Global Offensive, and a veritable leap into the electrified future of competitive recreation.    Permit me to set the stage: I am a gentleman of certain vintage, reared in the age of phonographs and dirigibles, when amusements were limited to lawn bowling, parlor theatricals, or perhaps a brisk game of chess beneath a gaslight. Imagine, then, my bewildered delight upon encountering this modern marvel—a game played not upon felted tables or polished wood, but upon an apparatus of glass and wires, illuminating wondrously with a kaleidoscopic vibrancy!    From the moment one enters the theatre of this digital war, one is swept away by its grandeur. The graphics—pardon, the visual presentation—is of such a quality as to inspire awe. The reflections upon marble floors, the delicate interplay of light and shadow, the minute details of bricks and bullet holes—all serve to transport the player into another realm entirely. It is as if one has been spirited away into a most daring operatic performance, where the overture is gunfire and the climax is ever at hand.    The gameplay—oh, what gameplay!—is a ballet of bullets and brain, a symphony of steel nerves and sharp reflexes. Teams of noble warriors, known colloquially as Terrorists and Counter-Terrorists, engage in a contest of cunning and coordination. Each round is a vignette of tactical precision: defusal of infernal devices, gallant rescues, and virtuosic marksmanship abound. The noble sport of fencing has nothing on the tense duels that play out in the alleyways of Mirage or the shadowy underpasses of Overpass. The pulse quickens, the breath shortens, and the soul stirs with excitement as one rounds a corner and faces fate head-on.    The newly implemented “sub-tick” system—though sounding rather like a term from an apiarist’s lexicon—is in fact a masterstroke of scientific advancement! It ensures that every shot, every footstep, every heroic leap is rendered with uncanny precision. No longer shall one cry foul at a missed bullet or an untimely demise! The code, like a conductor’s baton, guides each event with unwavering fidelity.    And the weaponry! A most impressive arsenal of armaments is made available to the player—rifles, pistols, grenades, and more—all modeled with such meticulousness that even the most seasoned officer would doff his cap. The AK-47, the noble M4A1-S, the thunderous AWP—each behaves with a character of its own, demanding both respect and mastery. This is no game of childish prattle; it is a gentleman’s contest, where skill reigns supreme and fortune favours the bold.    I must also sing praises of the camaraderie and competition found within the game’s online parlours—"servers," as the youth call them. There, strangers from all corners of the globe converge to test their mettle and forge bonds of rivalry and friendship alike. Though separated by oceans and continents, we are united in our shared love of clutch moments, clean headshots, and the ecstasy of victory hard-earned.    One must not overlook the game’s robust aesthetic charm. The music, stirring and martial, quickens the spirit. The interface, sleek and utilitarian, would impress even the most stern bureaucrat. The skins—yes, I said skins, decorative attire for one’s instruments of war—add a degree of flamboyant flair, allowing each participant to express their personal taste, whether they prefer understated elegance or unrestrained ostentation.    In conclusion, Counter-Strike 2 is no mere pastime. It is a triumphant testament to the heights of human ingenuity, a thunderous declaration that the spirit of competition, of courage, of brotherhood, lives on even in this strange new century. It has rekindled in me the joy of discovery, the thrill of the chase, and the satisfaction of hard-earned triumph.    To those still unacquainted with this electrifying pursuit, I say: tarry no longer! Engage at once with Counter-Strike 2, and you shall find your evenings transformed into chronicles of valor and glory.    With deepest regards and a heart brimming with joy,  _Perzeval_

Counter-Strike 2 – A New Era for a Legendary Franchise    Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) builds on the legacy of one of the most iconic competitive shooters in gaming history and delivers a refined, visually enhanced, and tactically immersive experience that will impress both veterans and newcomers alike. Powered by the Source 2 engine, CS2 takes everything players loved about Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO) and elevates it with modern graphics, smoother performance, and meaningful gameplay improvements.    The first thing that stands out is the visual overhaul. Maps like Dust II, Mirage, and Overpass have been reimagined with impressive attention to detail, better lighting, and more realistic materials. The updated visuals maintain the iconic feel of each location while enhancing immersion and visibility. Volumetric smoke is one of CS2’s most talked-about features, and for good reason—it dynamically interacts with the environment and player actions, creating new tactical possibilities. Flashbangs clearing smoke or bullets pushing smoke aside adds an exciting layer of depth that rewards skill and creativity.    Movement and shooting feel tighter and more responsive than ever. CS2 fine-tunes the classic mechanics of Counter-Strike without losing what made them so compelling. Gunplay is still crisp, recoil patterns are challenging but fair, and hit registration benefits from the newly improved server tick architecture (sub-tick updates), leading to more accurate and consistent gameplay.    One of the best aspects of CS2 is how well it balances nostalgia and innovation. Long-time fans will find familiar mechanics, maps, and weapons, but with small, intelligent changes that modernize the experience. Meanwhile, the improved user interface, match-making system, and overall polish make it easier for new players to dive in and learn.    The audio design also deserves praise. From the crisp gunshots to subtle environmental cues, every sound feels intentional and provides valuable information. The improved audio spatialization adds another tactical element to competitive play.    While CS2 is still receiving updates and fine-tuning, Valve has shown strong commitment to community feedback and ongoing development. Frequent patches, new features, and community involvement suggest a bright future for the game.    In conclusion, Counter-Strike 2 is a worthy successor to one of the most beloved competitive shooters in the world. It modernizes the classic formula in smart, respectful ways and sets a strong foundation for the next decade of tactical FPS esports. Whether you're a die-hard CS veteran or someone curious to try the series for the first time, CS2 is a must-play experience.    Rating: 9.5/10

I really don't think at this point in time Counter Strike is the game you should be playing if you want to play a competitive game. The game has been showing improvements since the launch of CS2 and the general quality of life has improved significantly since launch. Recoil updates, map fixes, stability, but as a player they feel more or less as the bare minimum for the actual quality of the game. They've added skins and cases, even a weapons pass and something should be said for these additions even if it pads their pockets.  However this game is PLAGUED with cheaters, play the casual modes but don't touch competitive or premier and even then you will absolutely run into someone cheating. If you want a game that your going to give call outs to your team and feel like you playing a game that respects you as a player unfortunately this game is not for you. BUT if you want to find out how good those cheats you downloaded for free are you'll get at least 3 months out of an account of rage cheating before ban. They give you plenty of time to dial it so after a couple of accounts if your getting banned its a skill issue.   This game as one point in time was one of the most competitive games to play and had a anti-cheat system while not perfect worked better to catch more cheaters in a shorter time. The first words in the demo are about how competitive the game has been over the last 20 years. Yet is appears that keeping the game competitive has taken a back seat. Totals suggest CSGO Overwtach was banning between 50k and 100k players a month compare that to the "more popular" CS2's 8k-30k. People didn't stop cheating Valve doesn't respect the player base enough to spend the money to remove them and don't think sites like FACEIT will save you.   And here lies the true problem the game is fun throwing smokes to cover A site and push in as a team feels rewarding, playing time so the bomb goes off feels rewarding, and the game will give you things that make it FUN but past a certain rank the likelihood you encounter a cheater climbs above 50% and the fun only happens 50% of the time. And this is not just from personal experience in me playing, this is a fairly common consensus from the pros and streamers who play this game.  Do i recommend it? Sure, like id recommend someone to get into painting, its fun, relaxing, something to do, but if you want to compete your probably gonna have to cheat simply because everyone else already is.

I would like to preface this by saying the following thoughts are based on my personal experience and perspective playing Counter-Strike 2's [CS:2] beta version. Counter-Strike: Global Offensive [CS:GO] has played a significant role in my life, and I offer these insights in the spirit of sharing my passion for Counter-Strike. As a player with over 8,000 hours invested in CS:GO since early 2014 and a past history in semi-professional play, with ~50 matches played on HLTV, my perspective may be influenced by my extensive time spent on CS:GO. I am now just a casual and washed-up player who plays with friends during my spare time.  I understand that the CS2 version is a limited-test, and not the full release. I have come into CS2 with an open mind and am fully aware that the game will still be in development and subject to changes. Therefore, I will discuss and evaluate CS2's current state compared to CS:GO.  Firstly, I'd like to consider some of the most important elements of CS:GO. While I won't delve into every aspect, I'll highlight key factors that can serve as reference points when discussing and evaluating CS2.  High Frame Rate and Optimised Graphics  CS:GO is optimised to run on a wide range of setups. We can often achieve fairly high and consistent frame rates on moderately powerful computers (with some optimisations). Further, CS:GO's graphics are finely tuned to strike a harmonious balance between visual quality and performance. This ensures that players with diverse setups can enjoy a seamless experience without compromising substantially on visual quality.  'Buttery Smooth' Feeling  Secondary to high frame rates, us players often describe the ideal CS:GO experience where everything feels exceptionally smooth, responsive, fast, and crisp. This is often attributed to other factors as well, including low-input lag and network infrastructure (i.e. 128-tick servers, responsive netcode, etc).  Movement  CS:GO's movement system feel intuitive, responsive, and quick. Character animations are smooth and fluid, allowing for advanced movements like bunny-hopping and strafing to feel seamless. This is a fundamental aspect of the game's competitive gameplay and contributes to the overall depth and skill ceiling of CS:GO.  There are many other factors which make CS:GO an elite first-person shooter game. However, after playing around 15 games of CS2, I can confidently state that there are numerous issues that need addressing.  Firstly, I think most can agree that performance is currently the biggest issue. The general consensus is that, even with optimisations, CS2 is not delivering with high and consistent frame rates. Although my PC is equipped to produce high frames, it is not able to constantly produce 300+ frames per second [fps] unlike CS:GO, which is producing 400 to 500 fps. I understand as games advance (i.e. Source 1 to Source 2 Engine) and technology evolves, the demand on hardware to deliver high frame rates and optimal performance will increase. CS2 is supposed to be an improved iteration of the game, yet it is marked by a concerning perception of poor performance. My gameplay experience should exhibit a smooth, swift, and crisp response, instead it feels noticeably delayed and lacks the fluidity and responsiveness expected. Further, there is noticeable stuttering and screen-tearing which feels like 60hz at times. Even though my system maintains a fairly high frame rate (i.e. 250 to 350 fps), the overall gameplay experience within CS2 resembles that of a considerably lower frame rate.  Secondly, it feels like the movement is quite 'sluggish'. I have switched between both CS:GO and CS:2 and the distinction is clear. The movement in CS2 is not yet refined to what Counter-Strike should feel like, and the input lag which is evident makes aiming and moving feel delayed. From swapping between the two games, it feels like 128-tick is much more responsive and elegant compared to the current sub-tick system. This might just be me, but the current sub-tick system feels like a cheap version of 128-tick. Additionally, I have noticed that player animations seem unnatural when enemies wide-swing/peak. There is undoubtedly an elevated advantage for players who peek first compared to CS:GO. This may be related to buggy character animations, lag compensation, interpolation, server-side issues, etc.  Thirdly, there is a clear issue with spraying when compared to CS:GO. Spraying feels somewhat random, and pulling down does not consistently produce the desired recoil control. I'm not sure if this is an intended change though.  Fourthly, the audio when hearing footsteps and other in-game noises sound unclear and can be quite difficult to differentiate. This may be a me problem, but I've heard this has been an issue for many other players too.  I have noticed some other minor issues, which include rubber-banding with nearby players, not being able to pick up weapons easily, difficulty noticing health drops, smoke duration being too long, and shots feeling delayed. I understand, and trust, that Valve will fix many of these issues (and others I have not mentioned). However, my concern lies around some of the discussed significant issues, especially considering that the game is expected to be fully released soon. In essence, my experience with CS:2 can be summarised with the age-old adage: "if it ain't broke, don't fix it." It underscores the importance of preserving the elements that have made Counter-Strike iconic while carefully considering necessary improvements for a seamless transition to the next chapter of the franchise.  I'm not here to take a dump on Valve or their CS2 efforts, but as a long-term player of Counter-Strike I believe it is vital to preserve the core elements that make Counter-Strike the best game in the world. Accepting suboptimal performance as the norm is not conducive to the longevity and health of the game. If this trajectory persists, there is a legitimate risk of the game permanently suffering from performance-related shortcomings. I understand that change is needed to keep the franchise fresh and appealing to new players and audiences. However, it is crucial that these changes are made with careful consideration of the game's identity and the expectations of its dedicated player base. Finding a balance between innovation and preserving the core essence of Counter-Strike is essential to ensure that the game continues to thrive and maintain its status as one of the most iconic games ever made.

🎮 Counter-Strike 2 – A New Era with Familiar Firefights Counter-Strike 2 marks a major leap forward for one of the most iconic shooters in gaming history. Built on the Source 2 engine, CS2 delivers a graphical overhaul, improved responsiveness, and subtle gameplay refinements—while staying true to the hardcore, competitive spirit that defined its predecessors.  ✅ What’s Better in CS2 Visual Upgrade: Lighting, smoke effects, and maps have received a huge facelift. Maps like Dust2 and Mirage feel fresh without sacrificing layout familiarity.  Responsive Tick Rate: Valve’s new sub-tick system allows for more precise movement and shooting, making the game feel smoother and more responsive, especially in high-stakes duels.  Volumetric Smoke: Smoke grenades are now dynamic and interact with the environment and bullets. It adds depth and realism without breaking game balance.  Modern UI & Menus: Everything from the main menu to the scoreboard has been reworked for a more polished, modern look.  🤔 What Still Needs Work Performance Optimization: While Source 2 looks great, some users with mid-range PCs report FPS drops or stutters. CS2 can be demanding on older hardware.  Matchmaking & Cheating: Despite improvements, the matchmaking experience can still feel inconsistent. VAC Live is a step forward, but cheaters haven’t been fully eliminated.  Content Gap: Some community-favorite modes and maps didn’t make it at launch, and while updates are coming, the transition feels a bit thin for long-time players.  🧠 Final Verdict Counter-Strike 2 isn’t a radical reinvention—and that’s a good thing. It polishes the formula, modernizes the visuals, and paves the way for the next decade of competitive FPS action. Hardcore fans will feel at home, while new players can appreciate the smoother onboarding.  Score: 8.5/10 A must-play for competitive FPS fans, with room to grow as updates roll in.

Become a Pro at Yelling Instead of Calling Out  Communication wins matches in CS2—unless you're doing it wrong on purpose. Skip boring callouts like “two B.” Instead, after charging into a 1v5 and getting dropped, scream “DO I EVEN HAVE A TEAM?!” Bonus points if you blame the loss on the top frag who's been dead all round. For efficiency, make a key bind to spam “TRASH TEAM” instantly. Because nothing builds morale like audio spam full of insults.  Spray and (Mostly) Pray  Precision aiming? That’s for nerds. Just hold down mouse1 with your AK and let recoil RNG carry you. If you miss, say you were “setting up the trade.” Want to look like you're improving? Load up a recoil training map and pretend you're practicing. You won’t actually learn anything, but hey—it looks productive.    The Economy is Just a Suggestion  Round one? Insta-buy a Deagle because you know you’re cracked with it. Lose the round? Rush buy a P90 and storm B like it owes you money. Never save, and definitely don’t communicate your buys. Saving for an AWP is for people who don’t live on the edge. If your squad tries to coordinate an eco, mute them. They lack your fearless investment strategy.    Grenades Are Optional, Flashing Teammates Isn’t  Know one smoke lineup for street cred, then throw flashes at your teammates for dominance. Blinding your entry fragger? Power move. Molotovs? Best used to trap the bomb carrier or block rotates—just for laughs. Smokes? Yeet them at a random corner and call it “cutting off vision.”    Move Like a Legend (Badly)  Forget all that fancy talk about counter-strafing and movement mechanics. Crouch-walk like a stealth god—right into a headshot. Jumping? Slam crouch mid-air for that 1-in-a-million glitch clip. You’ll die, sure, but your commitment to the bit is undeniable.    Get Kicked, Win the Game  Want true infamy? Make your team hate you so much they vote you out. Mic spam “WHO TOOK MY PASTA?” or flash your squad every single round. Bonus: knife a teammate and say it was “muscle memory.” When the ban hammer drops, take it with pride—you made your mark.    Never Take the Blame  Whiffed your spray? Lag. Got bodied in a 1v1? Smurf. 2-15 stat line? Clearly cheating enemies and a broken engine. Immediately open a new thread titled “FIX CS2 NOW” and wait for the sympathy. Self-awareness is optional when deflection is this easy.    Your Knife Skin is the Real MVP  CS2 is about flex, not frags. Got a Karambit Fade? Inspect it mid-round and ignore everything else. Get fragged while looking at it? Worth. Remember skins equal wins.  Just Getting Warmed Up” Coping Strategy  Three bottom-frag games in a row? Doesn’t count—you’re still warming up. Accused of throwing? Just say you’re “trying new strats.” If they don’t buy it, challenge them to a 1v1—and immediately leave when you're down 3 rounds. Tactical repositioning, not quitting.    Lean Into the Madness  CS2 is part shooter, part emotional roulette. One match you’re a frag god, the next you’re being roasted by a kid who can’t vote. Counter-Strike 2 should be incredible. It has the legacy, the core mechanics, the player base — everything it needs to be a top-tier competitive shooter. But none of that matters when cheaters run wild and the developers do next to nothing about it.  You load in wanting to have a good match, maybe hit some nice shots, climb the ranks, have fun with friends. Instead, you’re constantly second-guessing whether that headshot was skill or another blatant spinbot with zero consequences. Wallhacks, aimlocks, you name it — and they’re in every rank, from silver to global. It’s exhausting.  VAC? Might as well be a scarecrow. The anti-cheat is outdated, slow, and clearly not catching anyone until days (or weeks) later — if at all. And even if someone gets banned, there’s nothing stopping them from making another account and ruining more games. Meanwhile, legit players get penalized for leaving lopsided matches, but cheaters just keep queuing like it’s nothing.  What’s worse is the silence. The dev communication is practically nonexistent when it comes to this issue. No meaningful updates, no roadmap for fixing ranked integrity, no community engagement around the one thing killing the game. It honestly feels like Valve’s just coasting off the Counter-Strike name while the community bleeds out.  And it’s a shame — because when it works, CS2 can be fun. The core gameplay still has that tight, clean, high-stakes feel. The gunplay is solid, the maps look great, and the movement feels smooth. But none of that matters if half your games are ruined by people not playing fair.  I want to love this game. I should love this game. But the total lack of action on cheating and ranked integrity is just killing it. Until Valve actually decides to care about the competitive experience, it’s hard to recommend CS2 to anyone who values their time or sanity.

I booted up Counter-Strike 2 with dreams of glory. I imagined clutching 1v5s, dropping 30-bombs, and having random teammates call me "GOAT" while soft music played in the background. What actually happened was a two-hour descent into digital humiliation, self-loathing, and getting headshotted so fast I thought I had early-onset narcolepsy.    Let me start with the good stuff:    • The graphics are chef's kiss. Never has dying looked this beautiful.    • Gunplay is tight, responsive, and absolutely unforgiving if you're a chimp like me with the reaction time of a microwave.    • Maps are sleek and polished, with plenty of nice corners to die in.    • Smokes are now volumetric. I don’t know what that means, but I do know I can’t see a damn thing anymore.    Now the bad:    • Everyone is either a pro or a sentient aimbot from Eastern Europe.    • I can't tell if I'm playing against humans or if NASA let their AI project run loose on matchmaking.    • My teammates insult me in six languages I don’t speak, yet I still feel the shame in my soul.    Hackers? Oh yeah, they’re here. They never left. They simply evolved. Gone are the days of the obvious spinbot doing 360s and blasting dubstep in mic. Now they’re subtle. Now they toy with you. They miss one shot on purpose so you get hope. Then they flick and dome you through a molotov, smoke, three crates, and your sense of self-worth.    Let me paint a typical round for you:    Match Start  I buy a P90 because recoil control is for cowards. Rush B. Immediate headshot through double doors. I hear "EZ" in chat from someone named "[RU]smoke_mid_idiot." Good start.    Mid-Round  Our team is down 2-7. One of my teammates is AFK, another is griefing by flashbanging us every round, and the third is telling me I sound like a "discount toaster." I say "gg" unironically.    Clutch Time  It’s 1v1. I’m last alive. My palms are sweaty. Mom’s spaghetti. I peak corner—bam, instantly deleted by a guy named “NotCheatingIPromiseLOL” who has a 100% headshot rate and plays like he's streaming from the Matrix.    End Game  We lose 3-16. I go 2-19. One of those kills was my teammate. I still get MVP for “Most Bomb Plants.” I never even planted the bomb. I think the game is trying to make me feel better.    Overall, Counter-Strike 2 is an absolutely amazing tactical shooter... if you're good. Or a cheater. Or ideally both. If you’re a regular scrub like me who just wants to play casually and have fun, prepare to have your will to live slowly headshotted out of your body round by round.    Would I recommend it? Absolutely. 10/10. Best masochism simulator on Steam. Just bring tissues, a thick skin, and an emotional support llama.    Final Verdict:  🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟  Five stars, mostly because I can’t figure out how to uninstall it.

I’ve been a long-time fan of the Counter-Strike series, but CS2 is an absolute disaster in its current state. The game is plagued with cheaters, and it’s gotten to the point where playing legit feels like you’re deliberately putting yourself at a disadvantage.  Nearly every other match has someone using wallhacks, soft aim, or blatant aimbots. It’s incredibly obvious—instant headshots through smokes, pre-firing angles with perfect timing, and players tracking you through walls like it’s nothing. And the worst part? Valve’s anti-cheat seems completely useless.  VAC has always been a meme, but in CS2 it feels like there’s no enforcement at all. Reporting cheaters does nothing, and there’s zero transparency or feedback. How is it possible that a AAA competitive shooter in 2025 still doesn’t have a functioning anti-cheat system?  It’s frustrating and demoralizing to lose games not because you’re outplayed, but because you’re up against blatant cheaters ruining the experience for everyone else. CS2 could be great, but right now it feels like a haven for cheaters and smurfs.  Valve seriously needs to get its act together. Until then, this game is unplayable. Save your time, sanity, and money.  Rating: 2/10 – Only gets points for nostalgia and graphics.  ---  UPDATE (June 1, 2025): Nothing has changed. If anything, it’s worse. CS2 still feels rigged—like you're playing a slot machine where the odds are stacked against anyone trying to play fair. Some matches feel outright scripted, as if the game is designed to keep certain players winning while others get buried under cheaters, broken matchmaking, and wildly inconsistent hit registration. Combine that with the flood of smurfs and account boosters, and you’ve got a game that feels more like a shady casino than a skill-based FPS. Until Valve seriously overhauls the anti-cheat and matchmaking systems, CS2 will remain a joke in the competitive gaming scene.  UPDATE (June 2, 2025): Still no improvement. Cheaters continue to dominate ranked games. VAC remains passive, matchmaking is a mess, and legitimate players are stuck in a cycle of frustration. Counter-Strike 2, the latest iteration in the renowned franchise, regrettably falls short of expectations due to several critical shortcomings that significantly impact the player experience.  The most pervasive issue is the prevalence of cheating. The current anti-cheat system, Valve Anti-Cheat (VAC), appears demonstrably ineffective against the widespread use of third-party software. This widespread cheating undermines the competitive integrity of matches, leading to a consistently frustrating and unfair environment for legitimate players.   Furthermore, the matchmaking system exhibits persistent flaws. Players frequently report highly imbalanced matches, suggesting inadequacies in the system's ability to create fair and competitive pairings. This often results in one-sided engagements, detracting from the strategic depth and enjoyment traditionally associated with Counter-Strike.  A critical area requiring immediate attention is player support and communication from Valve. There is a notable absence of direct, effective channels for players to report issues, provide feedback, or seek assistance. Reliance on public discussion forums as the primary avenue for communication is inefficient; it offers no guarantee that player concerns are being actively acknowledged or addressed by the development team. This creates a significant disconnect between the player base and the developer, leading to widespread dissatisfaction and a feeling of being unheard.  In conclusion, while Counter-Strike 2 retains the fundamental gameplay mechanics, the pervasive cheating, flawed matchmaking, and insufficient player support infrastructure severely hinder its potential and compromise the overall user experience. Addressing these core deficiencies is paramount for the long-term viability and success of the title.

Counter-Strike 2 isn’t a reinvention—it’s a refinement. Built on Valve’s Source 2 engine, this follow-up to CS:GO doesn’t aim to reinvent the wheel but instead shines it to a mirror polish. It’s a sleek, modern evolution of one of the most iconic tactical shooters ever made.  From the moment you load into your first match, the improvements are immediately apparent. Visually, CS2 is a significant upgrade. The lighting is dynamic and realistic, maps have been overhauled with greater clarity and detail, and everything from smoke grenades to blood decals has been reworked for maximum immersion. The new volumetric smokes, which react to gunfire and environmental changes, aren’t just pretty—they add a layer of strategy that feels both fresh and fitting.  But Counter-Strike has always been about precision, and thankfully, the core gameplay remains untouched where it counts. The gunplay is as tight and skill-dependent as ever. Spray patterns still matter, positioning and communication still win rounds, and the economy still shapes your every decision. Veteran players will feel right at home, while newcomers are greeted with a more streamlined, modern experience.  Latency and tick rate—long-standing community concerns—have seen improvement thanks to “sub-tick” updates. While it’s not a magic fix, the responsiveness of movement and shooting feels snappier and more consistent, particularly in high-stakes firefights.  Where CS2 falters slightly is in its launch content. At release, not all modes or maps made the jump, and some features from CS:GO felt missing or undercooked. That said, Valve has been steadily updating the game, and the foundation here is clearly built for long-term growth.  What’s most impressive is how CS2 manages to feel like both a modern shooter and a love letter to its 20-year legacy. It doesn’t chase trends; it doubles down on what made Counter-Strike great in the first place—pure, unfiltered competition.  Counter-Strike 2 is a confident, polished evolution that respects its roots. It might not change everything, but it doesn’t need to. For fans of high-stakes, high-skill shooters, it’s still the king of the hill—just with sharper edges and better lighting.  Rating: 8/10

In pixels born from legacy, where once a giant stood,  Came CS2 with promises of balance, art, and good.  The banners waved, the trailers sang of revolution nigh,  Yet what we found was something else a broken lullaby.    From Counter-Strike’s old beating heart, where legends shaped their fate,  Now rises ash and fractured code, too late to innovate.  What once was pure a tactical ballet of skill and mind   Is now a maze of malfunctions, by careless hands designed.    Each round begins, and hope is high until the truth unfolds.  A cheater spins, his script precise, his aim forever cold.  I lead in kills, I top the match, I do my part and more,  But every game is still a loss each round a closing door.    With wallhacks keen and toggled aim, they glide like spectres through,  While Valve looks on in silence still, with not a word or clue.  The anti-cheat, if it exists, must sleep beneath the sea,  For even bots in Deathmatch now are modded endlessly.    I dodge, I juke, I try my best the battle feels surreal.  A bot with movement like a god, who cannot miss nor feel.  And every task, each simple goal be it weekly quest or grind   Is drowned beneath the cheating tide we’re forced to leave behind.    But worst of all, the grandest sin the subtick system’s shame,  Sold as a gift, a breakthrough vast, yet weak beneath its name.  A miracle on paper, yes, precision once again!  But in the game it fails and flails, a phantom in the rain.    For bullets pass through heads unscathed, though sights are set with care.  You fire first, yet somehow die a death that spawns from air.  The servers twitch, the hitreg skips, the peeker's joy preserved,  And subtick lies like fallen kings whose power was undeserved.    I shoot, I swear, I scream aloud my aim was not astray!  But what’s the use of skill and form when netcode goes away?  What madness forged this ticking beast that tells us “You were slow,”  While death arrives from future frames we never saw or know?    And where, I ask, are shepherds now who once the field maintained?  The architects of gun and map, who once so proudly reigned?  Valve, once known for polish, care, for legacy and might,  Now lingers in the background mist, avoiding every fight.    There’s no response, no dev in sight, no patch that makes things right.  The cheating grows, the gameplay rots, the ranks are void of light.  We cry for change, for simple truth, for action swift and bold  But laughter echoes through the halls of studios grown cold.    The list goes on, the wounds run deep how tragic this has grown:    Matchmaking flawed, with ranks mismatched, and smurfs too freely thrown.    Poor optimization, frame drops in crucial strife,    A UI clunky, half-complete, that chokes the game's own life.    Maps that lost their soul and charm, though graphically refined,    Yet crates get updates weekly, as if we wouldn’t mind.    Crashes mid-match, inputs lagged, a killfeed stuck in glitch,    While skins and cases thrive, untouched by balance switch.    Sound design, once surgical, now muddled, late, or gone,  Where footsteps whisper far too close, or vanish with the dawn.    Ranks decay without good cause. Stats vanish without sound.    And worse the ban reports ignored, while real cheaters still stay,  As though integrity and pride have long since gone away.    And yet… I play. I still log in. I aim. I check my sight.  For buried in this wreckage lies a spark that once burned bright.  A game of gods, of duels intense, of smokes and clutch and plan,  Now trapped in hands that look away and leave the fire to fan.    This poem is no rage alone it is a plea in verse,  For something great, now left to rot, could yet reverse the curse.  Let devs descend from clouded towers, to listen, fix, and mend,  And build again a worthy game where skill can once ascend.    So here I end, not with goodbye but with a waiting sigh,  For I still dream of that pure match where fairness could apply.  Until that day, I queue again, with friends and foes alike,  In servers flawed, with passion worn, still chasing the old strike.    May Valve one day remember us the players still who care,  And walk the halls of Counter-Strike with craftsmanship and flair.  For now, we weep in lyrical form, but one day we might cheer  If CS2 becomes again the game we once held dear.

CS2 promised to be the evolution of the legendary Counter-Strike, but somehow it feels like the developers handed us a game and said, “Here, fix it yourself.”  First off, the graphics look amazing — until you realize that now you can actually see your enemies hiding behind literally every pixel of scenery. Suddenly, every bush is a death trap and every corner is a “surprise, you just lost.”  The new engine is so fancy it somehow managed to make every grenade feel like a lottery ticket. Throw a flashbang, and pray you don’t blind yourself. Throw a smoke, and it either vanishes like magic or chokes your own team like a cheap vape.  The hit registration? Oh boy. Sometimes I feel like I’m playing whack-a-mole with bullets that bounce off enemies like they’re made of rubber. I’ve fired entire clips into a guy’s chest only for him to turn around and headshot me with a single bullet. Magic, or maybe witchcraft.  Matchmaking feels like a cruel joke. One game, you’re paired with a team of pros who communicate like a well-oiled machine. The next, you’re stuck with people who think the bomb is a lunchbox and the defuse kit is a fashion accessory.  The in-game economy is still there, because apparently, we needed more things to stress about besides whether your teammates will TK you or not.  And the new CS2 features? Sure, the map designs are tighter, but now it feels like every player is a ninja who can teleport faster than you can say “rush B.”  Final Rating: 3 smokes gone wrong out of 5 CS2: Come for the nostalgia, stay because you accidentally queued up and can’t escape. Still better than real life, but barely.

Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is not just a game — it's a cultural phenomenon. Since its launch, CS:GO has stood tall as one of the most competitive and skill-demanding shooters on the planet. Whether you're clutching a 1v5 or missing every AWP shot in warm-up, the game delivers a high-stakes adrenaline rush unlike anything else.  ✅ What Makes CS:GO Great: Flawless Gunplay: Every shot counts. The mechanics reward precision, strategy, and lightning reflexes.  Map Mastery: Learning callouts like "long", "cat", and "banana" becomes second nature. Each map is a finely tuned battlefield.  Endless Skill Ceiling: No matter how good you are, someone is better — and they're probably smurfing in your game.  Economy Meta: CS:GO’s buy system adds a chess-like layer of strategy. Spend wisely, win rounds, tilt enemies.  Esports Legacy: Watching pros make it look easy only to realize you’ve been flashbanging yourself for 3 years straight is... humbling.  🎧 Multiplayer Voice Chat Experience: Now let’s talk about the real soundtrack of CS:GO: your teammates.  “RUSH B CYKA BLYAT!!!” Ah yes, the universal call to arms. Nothing says "we're going in" quite like a high-pitched Russian war cry through your headset at 3AM.  Expect random karaoke, intense breathing, conspiracy theories, and political arguments — often all from the same player in the span of a single round.  Russian, Polish, Turkish, Brazilian, American — no matter the region, someone will scream at you, and it’s usually your fault, even when it’s not.  Pro tip: Muting the entire team can be good for your mental health. But then again, you'd miss the accidental comedy gold.  💥 Final Verdict: 9/10 CS:GO is a masterpiece of FPS design — but also a social experiment gone horribly (and hilariously) right. If you can handle the learning curve and the occasional Slavic soundwave assault, you'll find one of the most rewarding competitive shooters ever made.

I understand "Die hard" csgo players don't want the game mechanics changed and blah blah blah, but to have a game that has been out for LONGER THAN SOME PLAYERS HAVE BEEN ALIVE and change NOTHING about it is absurd. This game has been alive long enough to watch the TWIN TOWERS COLLAPSE, and yet in their rebranded "CSGO2," All they have added is better graphics and one or two new maps. I would like to be able to click and hold to aim like every other first person shooter, but no we can't have that, can we? "Its not what we are used to" that's why its a SETTING. You CHANGE IT if you WANT TO. Fine whatever.      Moving on to gameplay. Deathmatch can get pretty annoying especially for new players, as the game mechanics are totally different than 90 percent of first person shooters and require you to un learn everything you have ever known in first person shooters. The bigger problem is you have players who have played for years, and you always have at least one in every casual or deathmatch that you play, and they play the game like they are a COD veteran playing in a lobby of Recruit level bots. You so much as step one step forward and there are three holes in your head where your brain used to be. Next, casual. Casual isn't terrible in terms of player skill. Some players are discovering how to turn left for the very first time and it makes it fun to play against others that are also newer to the game. The problem is they ignore the rules of every other game mode in the game and make it a 10v10 lobby almost every single time. Imagine rush hour traffic in Chicago Illinois. That, but as a first person shooter is what the 10v10 matches are sometimes.   Now for competetive.  Competetives are a fan favorite. Traditional rules, considering economy when purchasing different loadouts, etc. Its great. One *minor* flaw; The RANKING system. Explain how someone like me, who grew up playing first person shooters and plays cs all the time in his freetime to try to get better, can come across players at the LOWEST RANK IN THE GAME and get absolutely fucked. Im talking 3 pixels on my monitor are lit up and I immidiately fall dead on the ground. I walk around a corner, headshot. I open an entire clip standing perfectly still burst firing for accuracy and still somehow manage to lose duels head on. Youd think these people are MASTERS but nope they are people who have played this game for only "100" hours and are only silver(lowest) rank. Its one thing when you bounce back and fourth between wins and losses, but when you have SEVERAL GAMES IN A ROW where you go from winning 9 to 6 to 1 to 9 for several rounds in a row. When you go from barely winning to getting stomped and not having a chance to get a shot off some rounds to the point where you can't even fire one single shot some rounds and yet you are playing "ranked," a game mode that is supposed to fairly sort you into different ranks so you play against people of your similar skill level. Worst ranking system out of any game I think i've ever played in my life.  Lastly, game customization. WHY DO THEY HAVE CONSOLE COMMANDS? Who the fuck expects people playing a casual first person shooter game to know how to run commands just to personalize their game and their hud? If you want to ajust where your viewmodel and fov are, it should be a SETTING. Fucking MINECRAFT has settings for fov and viewmodel and cs is 10 YEARS OLDER than minecraft.  Graphics are okay in cs2, but for some of the other games that have come out recently by corporations just as big or even smaller, cs is definately lacking in terms of peak graphical quality. It was a long awaited update for cs2 graphics, but I don't know why they had to make it a "new game" when they didn't really change any mechanics. Its the same game I remember playing 5-10 years ago.  Lastly, paying money for cosmetics? Fine. Paying money for custom maps or guns? Whatever. Paying money to UNLOCK THE RANKING SYSTEM so you can actually play the game without getting paired against really good players randomly every match, and then STILL getting paired against those players because of their shitty ranking system is EXTREMELY frusterating.  The only reason I still play this game is because it is a moderately entertaining cheap game that I have that I can play with friends. I expected a little more from a game that is now over 25 years old and has a huge team of devs that have the power to implement things into the game that people want and chooses to worry about the things that some people simply don't give a shit about.  If steam had a rating system, I would rate it 2 stars out of 5, or a 4 out of 10. Not the worst game I have ever played, but just disappointed that these problems still exist many years later in their "improved" "2.0" game.

It was the late '90s, a time when the internet still buzzed with the sound of dial-up modems and cybercafés were sacred temples for young gamers. That’s where I first discovered Counter-Strike. Back then, it was just a Half-Life mod — a simple idea: terrorists vs. counter-terrorists. But for me, and for many from my generation, Counter-Strike was much more than that.  I remember my first matches on maps like de_dust and cs_assault. Games full of adrenaline, improvised strategies, and shouting between friends whenever someone pulled off an epic play… or died in the dumbest way. But it was also in those servers where I met the people who, without realizing it at the time, would become my best friends.  As time passed, we grew up. We studied, worked, moved away, some of us became parents. I now have several kids, responsibilities, a life that no longer revolves around spending afternoons at a LAN café. But one thing hasn’t changed: I still play Counter-Strike. Not every day, of course. Sometimes once a month, maybe twice. But always with the same friends. We log in, even if it’s just for an hour, and we’re back to being those kids from the 2000s — yelling through our headsets, laughing at silly moments, and coming up with absurd strategies that never actually work.  The most beautiful part is that now my kids watch me play, asking about that “old game” I like so much. Some of them have even started playing it too. I tell them that thanks to Counter-Strike, I have my best friends. That it was more than a game; it was a bridge between eras, a bond that’s lasted decades, a space where we’re still ourselves, no matter how much our lives change.  Counter-Strike didn’t just define a gaming era — it defined a part of my life. And as long as I can lift a mouse and hit the “buy AK-47” key, I’ll be there, in the server with my lifelong friends. Because some matches, simply, never end.

Counter-Strike 2 didn’t ruin my life. I handed it over willingly.  And I’ll probably log in again tonight. Just one more match. Maybe one more case.  Just one more.

Counter-Strike is hands down the best competitive game ever made. It's simplicity allows balance that is virtually impossible to find in any other competitive game in the gaming scene. The combination of the needed individual skill, team communication and teamwork to play at the highest levels is unmatched. For a new player, Counter-Strike is probably a daunting experience at first. The amount of skill expression seen in Counter-Strike can prove to be a steep slope to tackle as an inexperienced player facing others with hundreds if not thousands of hours played. Stick with it and you will realize that it's not about anything other than your own technical skill, knowledge and ability to work with other players that is holding you back. However, it is not a perfect game. If you don't want to face cheaters, ever, then you will probably have to play via faceit or some other client, which will be extra challenging for new players. Another thing to point out is the importance of specifically teamplay and team communications to win games, which can be lacking in the lower ranks of CS and be a source of irritation for a lot of players who want to climb the ranks. Finding players who you have good chemistry with and playing with them is a good alternative, at any rank. Furthermore there is a big incentive to gamble in order to have cool looking gun-, glove-, knife- and operator skins, which I'm personally against. I only recommend this game to non-casual players. Sure, there are a lot of community made maps and servers and whatnot, which can offer a more casual gaming experience which I have personally spent a lot of time on but Counter-Strike really shines in the simple competitive format. Whatever you want to sink your teeth into, expect to spend a lot of hours to get the gist of it.

CS2 Review: A Fresh Coat of Paint, But Is It Enough?  Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) is Valve’s long-awaited sequel to the legendary CS:GO, and while it brings some solid improvements, it’s not without controversy.    The Good:  Graphics & Engine: CS2 runs on the Source 2 engine, which gives the game a much cleaner, more modern look. Maps like Dust II and Mirage feel familiar but look sharper, with better lighting and improved textures.    Responsive Smokes: One of the standout features is the dynamic smoke system. Smokes now react to bullets and grenades, opening up fresh strategies and making gameplay feel more alive.    Tickless Servers: Valve’s new sub-tick system is meant to make hit registration more consistent. It’s a technical improvement, though some players still debate if it truly feels better in practice.    The Mixed:  Gameplay Changes: CS2 keeps the core Counter-Strike feel but makes subtle tweaks to movement and shooting. Some players feel it’s smoother, others say it’s clunkier. It depends on who you ask.    UI & Sounds: The new interface is sleeker but takes some getting used to. Weapon sounds and effects have been updated—some love them, others miss the old feel.    The Bad:  Performance & Bugs: At launch, many players reported FPS drops, stuttering, and bugs. Valve has been patching frequently, but performance still varies by system.    Missing Features: Not all content from CS:GO made it over yet. Some maps, modes, and community features are still absent, which makes it feel like CS2 isn’t fully done.    Final Verdict:  CS2 is a promising upgrade to a legendary franchise. It looks better, adds some cool tech, and keeps the core gameplay mostly intact. But it still feels like a work in progress. If you're a CS:GO veteran, you'll likely be torn between appreciating the improvements and missing what’s been lost (or hasn’t been added back yet).    Rating: 7.5/10 – Good, but still loading... Counter-Strike 2 Review: A Tactical Evolution With Mixed Results Rating: 7.5/10  After over a decade of domination by Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, Valve has finally released Counter-Strike 2, a long-awaited successor built on the Source 2 engine. While it brings undeniable visual upgrades and under-the-hood improvements, CS2 feels more like an overhaul than a true sequel—and that’s both its strength and its weakness.  Graphics and Engine Overhaul The most noticeable change is the jump to the Source 2 engine. Maps are brighter, more detailed, and have improved lighting and physics. Smoke grenades now react dynamically to gunfire and environmental changes, introducing new tactical possibilities. Animations are smoother, and weapon models look fantastic, giving the game a modern feel without sacrificing its competitive edge.  Gameplay and Mechanics Core gameplay remains unchanged—and for good reason. CS2 still thrives on precision, communication, and strategy. However, some mechanics have been refined. Movement feels slightly different (to the frustration of long-time players), and hit registration has seen improvements. Valve introduced subtick servers to enhance responsiveness, though the real-world impact has been inconsistent, and some pros argue that it hasn't lived up to expectations.  Maps and Modes Classic maps like Dust2, Mirage, and Nuke return with visual upgrades, but many players miss popular community maps and modes that haven't yet made the transition. The lack of features like Arms Race, Flying Scoutsman, or custom servers at launch disappointed a portion of the community.  UI and UX The user interface has been cleaned up and modernized. The new buy menu feels more intuitive and flexible, but also drew some criticism for breaking years of muscle memory. Stat tracking and player profiles are improved, but still somewhat barebones compared to what third-party tools offer.  Community and Transition Perhaps the most controversial part of CS2 is how Valve handled the transition. CS:GO was entirely replaced by CS2, leaving players no way to revert. Many community servers, mods, and competitive leagues were disrupted. The game is still stabilizing, and updates have been rolling out to address bugs, performance issues, and balance concerns.  Verdict Counter-Strike 2 is a promising evolution of the iconic shooter, but it feels like a work in progress. It preserves the tactical brilliance of its predecessor while modernizing its visuals and systems. However, rough edges, missing features, and a forced transition have made the launch rocky. If Valve keeps listening to the community and iterating, CS2 could easily cement itself as the future of competitive FPS. For now, it’s a solid—but not flawless—upgrade.

When I give this game a thumbs up, I give it that for people like me.  I'm an adult now, I've been around CS since I was around 11, back when CS:S was the main thing. CS:S was scattered in gameplay, didn't really have centralized matchmaking and actually trying to play the game as intended was difficult. I mainly messed around in gun game lobbies or TTT, and I mainly bought it to expand my Garry's Mod assets at the time.  Then CSGO came out, and with me being a teenager that liked shooting things I took a swing at it, and got started with Vanguard. I had played a lot of competitive FPS's up to that point but CS had hit the primal urge that all the others were born from. CSGO was in spirit the perfect sequel, and read this further if you want that to make sense.  Halo > Halo 2; H2 is regarded as one of the greatest sequels ever and the reason for that is that it innovated on already existing content of the original, added new content that kept up in spirit with the OG, and was an overall outstanding iteration on the original formula. In this sense, CSGO was the perfect sequel to whatever you could call the OG, whether it be CS:S or CS 1.6; or the combination of both (I'll let the monkeys argue over that in the comments.)  So, now I'm gonna circle back to what I said in the beginning, "When I give this game a thumbs up, I give it that for people like me."  CSGO had the innovation of proper loot cases (or whatever synonym you can come up with across other games), with skins that were unlike any other attempt at the concept (floats, wear, patterns, etc.), and this created a player-driven economy that the developers get to skim off of in their own self-created ecosystem. A concept that other publishers have tried to make poor imitations of in various ways (Just buying the skins, lesser forms of cases, etc.) In terms of innovation (or invention in this case) Valve knocked it out of the park. This is my problem though, I was 17 when I got into the game, and despite being well under gambling age, I definitely bought cases, keys, and spent many of my minimum wage fast food job paychecks fueling my desire to unbox a knife. In this aspect I think that being an adult now makes this more acceptable, but at the time not-so-much, there were better things for my 17 year old self to preoccupy himself with.  -------------------------------------------------------  This all aside, let's talk about CS2 objectively, and not from the rose-tinted glasses that many others seem to have over CSGO.  CS is one of those games that if it experiences even a minute change the community will collectively empty their bowels wherever they read the patch notes. In the car, at school, in bed, you name it, I can near-guarantee a passionate rant based out of hatred about the patch notes is soon to grace your eyes (even though they barely skimmed the notes and took to reddit to see what they should hate about it.) AK's and M4's must always be balanced this way, maps must stay predictable and anything new throws out their game sense. I'm not going to entertain these thoughts, a lot of the changes in CS2 are good, and resisting change in the first place is foolish. Everything changes, progress is constant.  The new smoke mechanics are astounding, and Valve is one of the first in the industry to attempt these new particle physics, I mean come on, people shooting through smoke giving away their location? Grenades clearing it temporarily? This adds new layers to the gameplay and most importantly the strategy, and like a perfect sequel it does it in amazing ways that doesn't compromise the spirit of what CS has going on for itself.  New additions to maps like Dust 2 have kept it interesting, the jump from CT to Cat is a great change, and it's a tasteful addition to the routes you can take to cat from A, mid, doors, CT, or even from car pushing back to CT should you not have the luxury of going down long to watch over the site. While a good portion of the community doesn't like this change, I'll tell them that it's not like they created a ladder going straight from the back of CT up to catwalk. The box jump takes time, it's risky, it's loud, and it really makes you vulnerable, the convenience to risk is balanced and that's what you have to look for when seeing if things like this are good changes.  At first I was hesitant about the armory passes, but I think that it's a good change of pace for monetization in CS. Battlepasses that aren't timelocked, you can redeem the points for a swing at anything in that dedicated store, you can have multiple of them, and the skins behind them aren't total dogwater either. Though I do wish they had stat-trak, I'm not gonna complain about a FN Long Dog should I ever finally unbox one.  The new lighting is mostly good, I think the CSGO art style was good don't get it twisted. After reviewing the before and after on Mirage for instance it is quite nice to have the inside of palace be lit up and not so dreary or dark. CS2 feels less like the source games of yore and has jumped forward with Source 2. The light bouncing and the vibes of the interiors of many of these maps has improved greatly with the new lighting. I did say mostly good, and this is because I do agree with others that it can be washed out in places. Right there at palace, the interior is nice, but once you walk out over firebox the plywood's detail is hard to see and the colors kind of blend together. I can easily see how this would cause some issues with gameplay, visibility, and being able to suss out the enemy. The skins are another issue, these skins were made for a darker world palette, and lighting too, so in cases of skins like a printstream the vibrant pearlescence is washed out and doesn't look as good as it did in CSGO. In a game where the skins are what make the majority of the money, this is problematic.  Though, I must say that the gameplay is still amazing, and the launch issues many complained about have mostly been rectified (mostly as in I can't find any of them anymore but I'm sure others will nitpick), subtick is still an issue but I don't really have this issue very often, like once every 20-30 games. It's non-consequential to me.  -------------------------------------------------------  CS2 is the perfect sequel to CSGO. The original core gameplay is here (as in nothing has been taken out), and the additions they've made have only made it better. New smokes are cash money, the map changes are pretty great too, the lighting is mostly good but struggles in other places (Reminder, Halo 2 was also like this but a bit worse in that dept.)  The reason this game is good for a person like me is that it has all the fixtures that I'd want, and that is appropriate for me. Skins/Gambling, who cares I'm in my late 20's now, I can make these decisions as a responsible adult. The strategy, gameplay, and patience required is ultimately the tempting aspects of gameplay that keep me playing it or bringing me back. The friends I play with, and the fodder I get to shoot at, are also some amazing things I enjoy about it. (Fodder as in: Impatient teenagers who hold W and don't like to think beyond 5 seconds ahead. Atleast that goes for most of you :^) )  Nostalgia vision is a bitch, and after seeing the content put out by others saying they grew up with CSGO, I get it man, I really do. I watched Halo go from peak to dogwater in a matter of a decade, I get the fear and hesitance that comes with change. The circumstances are different here, the game is great, the gameplay is fun, the skins are cool and the skills that you build here are to me pretty valuable in gaming.  CS is far from a "dead game" like many were saying before Armory pass update hit. Cheaters are everywhere and CS is unfortunately not an exception, but I am reviewing the game at its core before I am hit by a tirade of "cheaters bro cheaters" yes man, I get it, cheaters.  CS2 is a great sequel, nostalgic redditors be damned.

I still remember the first time I loaded up CS2, back when my children were laughing in the next room. Each round felt alive, every echo of footsteps carried the possibility of triumph or defeat. In that moment I was not just a player seeking a quick win, I was a parent soaking in a few spare minutes of joy before bedtime stories and bedtime prayers.    The core gameplay is as tight and precise as ever, with each shot carrying weight and intention. The maps are vibrant canvases where strategy and instinct collide in the best possible way. I still marvel at the smooth transitions between rounds and the way the community rallies around a clutch play. Even now I find myself searching for that spark of excitement that once lit up our little living room, and CS2 delivers it with startling clarity.    Of course it is more than just pixels on a screen. For me the game has become a living memorial to those moments when we shared laughter and simple victories. Whenever I log in I feel them beside me, cheering me on or playfully teasing my missed grenade toss. It is a strange comfort to know that even though they are no longer here, our shared passion lives on in every match I play.    Looking ahead I see CS2 growing stronger, evolving, and drawing in new players who will create their own memories and maybe some day look back on their own simpler times. The sense of community remains as strong as ever and I believe that this title will carry on for years to come, a digital gathering place where joy and skill join hands, and where memories—both happy and bittersweet—find a home.

At one point this was my thing but not anymore. If it's your thing still that's cool.  I was uninstalling this and the 80gb of storage space floored me enough to write this. The original was 20gb, for reference. There's so much bloat that it caused my face to twist when I realized how much space was wasted on a game I don't play anymore. And that was when I wrote this.  Like I used to have a lot of fun playing on the original (inaccessible still) CSGO, and all of the workshop maps associated with it. Lost to time now, most of them. I used to even enjoy competitive, quite frequently too (My record was Gold Nova Master before one of the great ELO/matchmaking changes).   And I guess I got older, the game just makes me very angry now, frustration is a big driver for improvement here. But I can't say for sure what it is even that makes me feel so bad playing this game. I stopped playing roughly around when they changed most of the gun sounds, and there's been a truly extraordinary amount of updates since then.   Source 2 is also a very impressive upgrade. However for my personal taste there's something now missing from the game visual style. It feels like 2006 again when every developer got access to the bloom setting and used it so often gamers got sick of it. The UI change feels weird to me and I can't navigate the menus anymore and I don't have the inclination as it is anyway to learn where all of the buttons went.   It doesn't help that this game seems almost predatory. Skins, gambling, and real cash are permanently attached to the game now and it's been that way for a very long time. You certainly do not need them to play, but very often you will find people obsessed with skins and the skin market. I own some myself, some skins are quite pleasant looking and some offer stat tracking on the gun you have the stat track skin for.  And I deeply miss hosting my own servers and having my friends join to play Michael Myers, yknow? We'd get a bad comp match back then, and instead of going "we ball" or "run it back" we'd do something else in the game and cool before jumping back in. Now the game only feels focused on further developing this competitive community. Which I suppose is fine? Even though I feel a sense of revulsion anytime I meet someone who takes competitive CS2 seriously now, same extends to many competitive games. And I know that's a personal feeling.   I think the only thing I can take away from this is something basic, the game will not remember the people like me who played it differently. It will not remember all of the workshop maps, either. Among the missing maps were heavily scripted stories, a bank heist, a fantasy where you slay a dragon. Gone. Because CS2 needed to replace CSGO. The developers decided that both could not co-exist and thus wiped the face of the workshop clean.   The thing about those heavily scripted maps too was that I'm pretty sure the people that had made those were Russian. Those were made pre-war. Those workshop maps might be permanently lost, who knows what happened to the creator after so many years.  Remember this was Valve, by the way. Very well known for mod and community support at one point.  It's also the same Valve that let Bethesda attempt to monetize the Skyrim workshop over a decade ago now, we shouldn't forget that either and remember who to hold accountable for mistakes like this.   And I use mistake generously here. Sometimes it's not so easy to say.  Of course this entire review is based on memory, some relatively recent, I can't afford to give you a proper review of what the gameplay is like today, and it would date the review anyway. Neither can I truly explain the minutiae of how this game does not respect you nor your time. I want to say it uses the same method of keeping users that a social media platform does, keep the player irritated so that when they do improve the dopamine hits are enhanced. But that's speculative.  I don't think I've ever written a negative review for a Valve product.  I've never felt offended by anything they've done up until recently.   Must be that I'm real sick of the way we've been going for the past decade now. Maybe someone else remembers, maybe I've lost it.   I dunno, that's all I wanted to write.  ez pz lemon squeezy

I’ve been playing Counter-Strike since CS 1.3, when jumping off a box felt like parkour and buying an AWP didn’t mean you were toxic... just rich. I've crouch-walked through dust in 640x480, sprayed through walls in aztec, and lived through the trauma of CS:Source’s hitboxes. And now, here we are — CS2. A whole new chapter.  Let’s be real — CS:GO was already a masterpiece. But CS2? It’s like your favorite band released a remastered album... and also added fog, volumetric grenades, and occasionally let you fly into the sky during a bug. Progress.  Watching legends like Heaton, Potti, elemeNt, fisker, f0rest, GeT_RiGhT, JW, s1mple, and ZywOo, now Donk evolve through these versions is like watching Pokémon evolve — only with more screaming and flashbangs. I’ve aged, my hairline has receded, but my muscle memory still bunnyhops (in my dreams, anyway).  And yes, CS2 is beautiful. The gunplay is crisp, the visuals are stunning, and the buy menu? Oh, the BUY MENU. Remember when buying a deagle meant you were smart and broke? Now it feels like Wall Street: buy this, rebalance that, swap mid-game... I didn’t realize I needed an MBA to afford a loadout.  Still, every bomb plant, every last-second defuse, every accidental team flash — it’s all still Counter-Strike. The chaos. The clutch. The community (and the occasional kid with a mic louder than a flashbang). This isn't just a game — it’s my youth, my rage therapy, and my aim trainer rolled into one.  Verdict: 10/10, would get one-tapped again for nostalgia.

PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds isn’t a battle royale—it’s a 100-player stress simulator where the real winner is whoever keeps their sanity intact.    What PUBG Does to a Human Being:  You will:    Loot for 20 minutes just to get headshot by a guy named "xX_TwitchProneKiller_Xx" hiding in a bathroom.    Crash your perfectly good car into a pebble and explode (physics engine = war criminal).    Get third-partied more often than a messy divorce.    Die to the blue zone because you were too busy arguing about loot distribution.    Unload a full magazine into a guy, only for him to turn around and one-tap you with a pistol. (Desync? Skill issue? Both?)    The PUBG Experience in 4 Phases:  1️⃣ Hope - "This is my game! I’ve got an M4 and a 4x! Let’s go!"  2️⃣ Denial - "No way he saw me. I was COMPLETELY hidden in this grass."  3️⃣ Rage - "HOW DID HIS SHOTGUN HIT ME FROM 200M?!"  4️⃣ Acceptance - "I’ll just drop Pecado and die immediately like God intended."    Pros:  ✔️ Nothing beats the adrenaline of a final-circle 1v1.  ✔️ Gunplay so satisfying it makes other shooters feel like Nerf fights.  ✔️ The panic when you hear footsteps upstairs ("Is that a teammate… or Satan?").  ✔️ Miramar exists (for the 3 people who actually like it).    Cons:  ❌ The "PUBG Moment"™ - When the game decides you don’t get to win today.  ❌ Teammates who take your loot then die 10 seconds later.  ❌ Getting killed by a guy who hasn’t moved since 2017.  ❌ Spending 15 minutes looting just to die to a pan melee.    Final Verdict:  PUBG is like an abusive relationship—you hate it, you love it, and you keep coming back for more. One day, I’ll get that chicken dinner… but today is not that day.

When it launched in 2017, PUBG: BATTLEGROUNDS single-handedly ignited the battle royale craze and set the blueprint for the genre. Years later, it remains a gritty, tense, and highly rewarding survival shooter that continues to attract millions with its realistic gunplay and strategic depth.  At its core, PUBG drops up to 100 players onto massive maps where the goal is simple: be the last person or team standing. Unlike some of its faster, more arcade-style competitors, PUBG emphasizes realism and tactical play. Weapon recoil, bullet drop, and sound cues are meticulously modeled, making every firefight feel authentic and challenging.  Matches begin with scavenging for gear—guns, armor, medical supplies—while staying alert to other players and the ever-shrinking safe zone. The pacing ranges from tense stealth and survival to explosive firefights, often in unpredictable urban or rural environments.  The game features several large, diverse maps—from dense forests and sprawling cities to arid deserts and islands—each requiring different strategies and playstyles. Whether you prefer long-range sniping, close-quarters combat, or tactical positioning, PUBG offers varied environments that reward adaptability.  In addition to classic modes, the developers regularly introduce new limited-time events and modes to keep the gameplay fresh.  PUBG sports realistic visuals with detailed environments and weapon models. While not pushing the absolute graphical frontier, the art style supports gameplay clarity and immersion. The sound design is excellent, with footsteps, gunshots, and vehicle noises playing a crucial role in player awareness and survival.  Over time, PUBG has evolved through constant patches, quality-of-life improvements, and new content drops. The game boasts a large and passionate community, with robust competitive esports scenes worldwide. While it faces stiff competition, PUBG remains a staple for players seeking a more methodical and intense battle royale experience.  PUBG: BATTLEGROUNDS remains a cornerstone of the battle royale genre—offering realistic gunplay, strategic depth, and tense moments that keep players on edge. If you crave a slower-paced, skill-focused shooter where every decision counts, PUBG delivers an unparalleled survival experience.  Authentic, tactical, and endlessly suspenseful—PUBG is battle royale distilled to its rawest form.  Rating: 8/10
